title: Podcast with Joel Van Dyk, CTO/CISO and Co-Founder of Done. Quantum Security Limited - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Joel Van Dyk, a physicist and Wall Street CISO veteran who co-founded Done. Quantum Security, argues there is a timing gap: large banks need about ten years to replace their cryptography, while a cryptographically relevant quantum computer is most likely four to five years away. His PQC Done proxy is meant to shield traffic in the meantime. He says the right goal is permanent cryptoagility rather than a one-time migration, ranks quantum as the #2 CISO risk after AI, expects blockchain to be hit first, and takes a middle stance on QKD.

insights.claim: Van Dyk says the most conservative estimate for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer used to be 2035 and has moved to about 2029-2030.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: A pulled-in Q-day timeline compresses PQC budgets into the next 3-4 years, which helps PQC vendors.
insights.quote: The most conservative estimate right now used to be 2035, and has moved into about 2029, 2030.
insights.locator: The most conservative estimate right now

insights.claim: Van Dyk says two papers published around late March to early April solved much of the basic physics of quantum computing and mapped the threat models. In his view this turned building a CRQC into an engineering problem.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Once a problem is engineering rather than science, timelines become more predictable and shorter, so the risk of discounting Q-day grows.
insights.quote: And so that turned this endeavor really into an engineering problem.
insights.locator: But I don’t. All I know

insights.claim: Van Dyk says a big investment bank needs about ten years to replace its cryptographic plumbing, similar to Y2K, while a CRQC is most probably four to five years away. That leaves roughly a five-year protection gap.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: The gap creates demand for stopgap products such as proxies, gateways and managed PQC, which can be sold before full migrations.
insights.quote: well, you’ve got a five-year gap, and you need some protection for that
insights.locator: There’s a lot of plumbing

insights.claim: Van Dyk compares PQC migration to Y2K because it touches all hardware and software firm-wide, and says it is arguably harder because every crypto algorithm has to change, not just clock logic.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Expect cross-functional, multi-year PQC programs with large consulting and integration budgets at banks.
insights.quote: you’re not just changing the clock algorithms, you’re changing all the crypto algorithms
insights.locator: So knowledge is always something

insights.claim: Van Dyk argues that a one-time PQC migration is a misconception. Because quantum computers will eventually solve all current algorithms, firms need continual cryptoagility, rehearsed the way firms rehearse backup restores each quarter or year.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: This favors recurring-revenue crypto-management platforms (inventory, KMS, centralized crypto) over one-off migration projects.
insights.quote: all the algorithms we have now will eventually be solved
insights.locator: So that’s one of the biggest misconceptions

insights.claim: Van Dyk says firms must be able to replace a broken NIST algorithm within a couple of days or weeks. That requires an inventory of hardware, software and third-party vendors, plus centralized cryptography.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Centralized crypto services and crypto-inventory tooling are the base layer that buyers will need to purchase first.
insights.locator: Inventory is just the first good thing

insights.claim: Van Dyk warns that the industry cannot afford another Heartbleed-style scramble when an algorithm breaks, so swap-over drills need to be practiced in advance.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: An algorithm break without rehearsed playbooks would be a systemic operational-risk event for financial institutions.
insights.quote: We can’t have another Heartbleed situation where everyone’s running around not knowing what they’re doing.
insights.locator: We can’t have another Heartbleed

themes.theme: Blockchain is first in the blast radius

insights.claim: Van Dyk expects blockchain, which is built entirely on asymmetric encryption, to be the first target when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives in perhaps four or five years.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Crypto assets and the tokenization investments of financial institutions face concentrated quantum risk. Watch chains' plans to migrate signatures.
insights.locator: And then another big thing is blockchain

insights.claim: Van Dyk notes that many financial institutions have invested heavily in blockchain, and says that is why he works with Project Eleven, which he describes as having some of the best work and IP in quantum-safe blockchain.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Project Eleven is a name to watch in post-quantum crypto security.
insights.locator: And a lot of the FIs have

themes.theme: PQC Done proxy and the data exhaust

insights.claim: PQC Done is a quantum proxy that sits like a firewall and moves traffic entering and leaving the firm onto quantum-safe algorithms. This buys five to six years for deeper infrastructure upgrades.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Network-layer PQC wrapping is a quicker-to-sell product category than code-level migration.
insights.quote: It’s trying to provide a set of shields to hide the rest of the firm similarly to a firewall
insights.locator: And so that’s what this PQC Done

insights.claim: Van Dyk's proxy uses AI to package the traffic it sees into cybersecurity risk-management data. He says there is an endless hunger for that data because regulators require firms to show where their cryptography is and how strong it is.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: The second revenue stream may be compliance and audit data rather than the encryption itself, which is the moat to watch for PQC vendors.
insights.quote: there’s an endless hunger for that kind of data now
insights.locator: So the idea is to flip

insights.claim: Project Eleven is building a PQC key management system (KMS) from the ground up. Van Dyk compares cryptography to the steel bars sunk in New York's bedrock, meaning PQC requires replacing foundational infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Ground-up PQC KMS vendors are positioned to take the 'keys to the kingdom' layer that banks keep in-house.
insights.locator: Today I am doing consulting

insights.claim: Van Dyk ranks quantum as the second-highest CISO priority after AI. His reasoning: getting AI wrong makes you an also-ran, but getting quantum wrong could get you owned very quickly once a CRQC appears.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Quantum security spending will grow, but AI security spending will still come first in CISO budgets over the next few years.
insights.quote: if you don’t get quantum right, you could be owned in a very short time
insights.locator: One of my former colleagues told me

insights.claim: Despite calling quantum a clear and present danger, Van Dyk thinks firms still have about three or four years to get their quantum response in place.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Most PQC buying will happen in 2027-2030, a window to track vendor bookings.
insights.quote: it’s something you’ve still got three or four years to really get under your belt
insights.locator: So I definitely put it as number two

insights.claim: Van Dyk recommends combining quantum security and quantum opportunity in a center of excellence, as he did at State Street with Rob Otter (now at JPMorgan), because both need the same scarce code-literate skill set.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Banks with joint quantum centers of excellence (JPMorgan, HSBC) are likely to lead adoption, and their hiring is a signal to monitor.
insights.locator: So you want to work very strongly

insights.claim: Van Dyk finds that board risk and audit committees understand quantum risk well before executive committees and senior or middle managers do, and puts awareness near the tip of the first Gartner hype cycle.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Pressure from the top of the board could unlock PQC budgets before operational management pushes for them.
insights.locator: And I find that when I talk to boards

insights.claim: Van Dyk says confusion and misconceptions about quantum physics produce FUD in both directions, from 'any day now' to 'physically impossible', and advises financial institutions to hire a physicist who can separate signal from noise.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: Takes that quantum is imminent and takes that it is impossible are both unreliable, so in-house technical judgment matters more than headlines.
insights.locator: And it’s like, “No, no, there isn’t.”

themes.theme: Cloud pull and the QKD middle path

insights.claim: Van Dyk expects the quantum threat to push banks further toward AWS, GCP and Azure, because cloud providers have better tooling and can deploy quantum-safe cryptography faster than banks, whose IT is a cost center.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: PQC is another driver of bank cloud migration, which is positive for hyperscalers.
insights.quote: I’m going to answer that with a definite probably
insights.locator: Do you feel that the quantum threat

insights.claim: Van Dyk says mainframes holding a bank's books and key management systems are likely to stay in-house, because banks want to keep the keys to the kingdom themselves, which limits how much moves to the cloud.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: On-premises PQC KMS and mainframe crypto upgrades remain a separate addressable market from cloud.
insights.locator: A lot of banks still have their mainframe

insights.claim: On QKD, Van Dyk takes a middle stance: firms should pilot it and learn where it fits, as in the cross-border pilot between the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, but it should not come before fixing basic cryptography and completing an inventory.
insights.speaker: Joel Van Dyk
insights.so_what: QKD is still an exploratory budget line behind PQC, so vendors are likely to see pilots rather than large deployments in the near term.
insights.locator: I don’t see how we can do it today
